findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Adding a non-default method order() to the public CryptoProvider interface is a source- and binary-breaking change for every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation. Any downstream project with a custom CryptoProvider (an explicitly supported extension point, loaded via ServiceLoader) fails to compile against the new keycloak-common and throws AbstractMethodError at runtime under binary compatibility, blocking upgrades for those integrators.

[BUG] Removing the multiple-providers error and replacing it with order-based selection leaves ties resolved by arbitrary ServiceLoader classpath order, and both DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider declare order() == 200. A deployment that previously failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' (WildFly-provisioned installs where crypto/default and crypto/elytron are both on the classpath) now silently initializes one of the two tied providers depending on classpath ordering, so two identical installs can exhibit different crypto behavior (e.g., WildFlyElytronProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returning null vs DefaultCryptoProvider returning BC) with no error logged at INFO or above.

[ADVISORY] AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of KeyStore.getDefaultType() (the JDK default keystore provider, e.g. SUN), not a BouncyCastle provider, while 15 of its other methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. Any authz-client code path or user code that reaches CryptoIntegration.getProvider() and then calls getPemUtils(), getSignature(), getCertificateUtils(), etc. (the provider is now registered globally via META-INF/services and wins selection whenever crypto/default is not also on the classpath) gets UnsupportedOperationException/NoSuchAlgorithmException instead of working crypto, breaking JWT verification or TLS setup in standalone authz-client usage that previously worked when a real provider was on the classpath.

[ADVISORY] Baking the META-INF/services CryptoProvider registration into the authz-client jar itself means the AuthzClientCryptoProvider is discovered for every application that merely has authz-client on the classpath, not only when AuthzClient.create() runs. Any other library or server in the same JVM that calls CryptoIntegration.init() with a classloader that sees authz-client (e.g., a WAR bundling authz-client deployed on a server using its own crypto provider) can get AuthzClientCryptoProvider selected alongside or instead of the intended one — and since it throws UnsupportedOperationException for most operations, unrelated crypto calls in that process fail; the old 'multiple providers' guard that would have surfaced this misconfiguration is removed in the same diff.

[BUG] Ties in provider order() are resolved by ServiceLoader iteration order, making provider selection classpath-order dependent. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so any classpath carrying two of them (e.g. default + fips1402) previously failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' and now silently picks whichever the ServiceLoader enumerates first — a FIPS deployment can silently boot on the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider with no error or warning above debug level.

[ADVISORY] The new provider-sorting/selection behavior has no test anywhere in the diff. The diff changes a hard failure (multiple providers = IllegalStateException) into ordered selection and adds the order() contract to a public interface, but no test covers sorting, tie behavior, or the 'Ignored crypto providers' path; a regression in the comparator or the ServiceLoader enumeration breaks provider selection for every embedding (server and authz-client) with nothing to catch it. The only new test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) exercises ECDSA byte conversion, not provider detection.

[ADVISORY] The only test of concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a round-trip through the same provider's own decoder, so it cannot detect a DER encoding both methods get wrong in the same way. The test converts DER→concat→DER→concat and asserts the two concat forms match; if concatenatedRSToASN1DER emitted non-interoperable DER (wrong tag/length) while asn1derToConcatenatedRS parsed it back symmetrically, the test passes but a Keycloak server or any BC-based verifier rejects the produced JOSE signature. A test asserting the re-encoded DER verifies against the keyPair public key (or equals the original raw DER signature bytes) is the missing acceptance criterion.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM's default KeyStore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider, so the method's contract is silently violated. Any caller that uses CryptoIntegration in a process where the authz-client provider wins (standalone client, order 100 < 200 so only when no other provider exists) and requests the BouncyCastle provider gets e.g. SUN with no BC algorithms; code doing provider-lookup by BC OID or name fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException at runtime instead of at selection time.

[ADVISORY] readLength's bounds check compares the declared length against the total input size (limit), not the remaining bytes (limit - count), so it only rejects lengths that overshoot the entire buffer. For a nested element near the end of a corrupted signature, a length that overruns the current element but stays under the total buffer passes readLength and fails later in read() with a generic EOF IOException (or reads sibling bytes as content), losing the 'corrupted stream - out of bounds length' diagnostic and making malformed-signature errors harder to attribute; no test covers the overlong-length path.

[BUG] The diff silently deletes the hard failure on multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath, converting a startup misconfiguration error into a debug-level log line, changing server-wide behavior far beyond the stated authz-client intent. A Keycloak server deployment that previously refused to boot with two crypto providers on the classpath (an explicit safety check against ambiguous FIPS/non-FIPS crypto) now boots silently using whichever provider has the highest order(); operators running an unintended FIPS-ineligible provider get non-compliant crypto with no error, only a debug log they will never see at default log levels.

[ADVISORY] Adding the abstract method order() to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation breaks every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation at runtime with AbstractMethodError. Third-party or customer custom crypto providers compiled against the old interface load fine but throw AbstractMethodError when detectProvider's sorted() comparator invokes order(), turning a previously-working deployment into a runtime failure after upgrade; the diff shows no default method or migration note for external implementers.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs and discards two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances with their BigInteger writes before building the real sequence, dead code with no traceable requirement. The next maintainer reading the method assumes the two orphaned encoders (ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) lines) have an effect and preserves or 'fixes' them; deleting both lines changes nothing, failing the deletion test's bar for dead weight.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK default KeyStore provider rather than a BouncyCastle provider, a misleading near-no-op that will surprise any caller that trusts the method contract. Any code path in authz-client (or shared common code) that calls getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC-specific behavior (e.g., BC-only PKCS12 handling or EC curve support) silently gets the Sun provider instead; the method name promises something the implementation does not deliver and no caller in the diff exercises it.

[ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS accepts indefinite-length DER sequences because readSequence's `while (length > 0)` loop is skipped when readLength() returns -1, silently returning an empty list that then fails the size!=2 check instead of rejecting indefinite encoding explicitly. A caller passing a BER indefinite-length signature gets a generic 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' IOException instead of a precise indefinite-length rejection, complicating diagnosis; the bound also means a truncated first element that overruns the declared length reads past the sequence into following bytes rather than failing, but the final arraycopy bounds are the safety net.

[ADVISORY] The tests only verify the round-trip concatenatedRS -> ASN1DER -> concatenatedRS, never validating the ASN.1 DER output against a known-good encoding, so an encoder bug that round-trips consistently (e.g., non-minimal DER integer encoding) passes the suite. If ASN1Encoder emits non-canonical DER (e.g., negative or non-minimal INTEGER encodings), a real Keycloak server verifying the JWS will reject the signature while the diff's own tests stay green; the happy-path round trip cannot represent cross-implementation compatibility, which is the whole point of the ECDSA signature conversion.

[BUG] Adding a non-default abstract method `order()` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface breaks every existing third-party implementer at runtime with AbstractMethodError. Any out-of-tree CryptoProvider compiled against the old interface (SPI is a documented extension point — custom/alternative crypto deployments register via META-INF/services) now fails when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` invokes `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` on it during `CryptoIntegration.init`, which the diff makes AuthzClient.create call unconditionally — the previously-working authz client and the whole Keycloak startup path crash with AbstractMethodError instead of a versioned contract change. The method should have been a Java default method returning a sentinel.

[ADVISORY] The diff replaces the fail-fast 'multiple crypto providers on classpath' error with silent preference by order(), turning a previously-loud misconfiguration into a silent one, and ties are resolved nondeterministically. Operators who accidentally end up with two providers on the classpath (e.g. authz-client fat-jar plus the server's DefaultCryptoProvider) previously got an explicit IllegalStateException naming the conflict; now the loser is only a debug-level log line, so a deployment that silently routes crypto through the wrong provider ships to production. Additionally, three in-tree providers all return order()==200 (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider), so if two of them coexist the ServiceLoader iteration order — which is classpath-order dependent and unstable — decides which crypto stack (FIPS vs non-FIPS) is used, a selection no configuration controls.

[ADVISORY] AuthzClientCryptoProvider registers itself as a classpath-wide CryptoProvider service while 14 of its 19 methods throw UnsupportedOperationException, and getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default KeyStore provider rather than BouncyCastle. Any application that has authz-client on its classpath alongside another CryptoProvider of lower order (any third-party provider with order < 100, which is all pre-existing ones given they lack order() — though those already fail per the interface break; or a future low-order one) silently routes all crypto through a provider whose getPemUtils/getSignature/getCertificateUtils throw. Within authz-client itself, any code path beyond ECDSA signature conversion — e.g. PEM parsing of a client's signing key or the JWT client-credential flow — now calls into these stubs and crashes at runtime. The getBouncyCastleProvider() lie is worse than an exception: callers (including BouncyIntegration-dependent code in common) get a plain SunJCE/SunRsaSign provider where BouncyCastle-specific algorithm OIDs or the BC keystore format is required, producing NoSuchAlgorithmException far from the cause.

[ADVISORY] The only test for the new ASN.1 DER codec is a self-referential round-trip through the same encoder/decoder under test, never verifying the produced DER against an independent parser or a real signature. A symmetric encoding bug — e.g. the encoder emitting a non-minimal INTEGER or the decoder's indefinite-length path (`readLength` returning -1 makes `readSequence`'s `while (length > 0)` loop return an empty list) being mirrored on both sides — keeps the test green while real-world signature verification against a spec-conformant verifier fails; the guard can be green while interop is broken. A cross-check against BouncyCastle's ASN1Primitive or an actual JWKS verification would close it.

[ADVISORY] readSequence treats an indefinite-length BER encoding (readLength returns -1) as an empty sequence and returns successfully instead of rejecting it. asn1derToConcatenatedRS fed an indefinite-length signature (BER, which some signers emit) returns no parse error of 'indefinite length' but instead proceeds to the size!=2 check, and more importantly the `while (length > 0)` loop exits immediately producing a misleading error message — or, if the length check were absent, silently empty output. A caller debugging gets 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' instead of the actual BER/DER mismatch, and any future reader of this method can be led to believe indefinite length is handled.

[BUG] This diff silently deletes the fail-fast 'multiple crypto providers on the classpath' IllegalStateException contract from CryptoIntegration.detectProvider, replacing it with order()-based silent selection, without any explicit acceptance of that behavioral change to server-side code. Previously, a misconfigured server classpath containing both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider (or elytron) threw an IllegalStateException at startup, telling the operator exactly which providers conflicted; now it silently picks the highest-order provider and only logs 'Ignored crypto providers' at DEBUG level. A FIPS-required deployment that accidentally also carries the non-FIPS jar now silently runs the non-FIPS provider (both have order 200, selection among ties is ServiceLoader order, i.e. non-deterministic across environments) — a compliance/security posture change invisible to the operator, and a contradiction of the method's documented purpose of detecting provider conflicts.

[ADVISORY] AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK's default KeyStore provider, silently violating the CryptoProvider interface contract that this method returns the Bouncy Castle provider. Any common-code path that calls getBouncyCastleProvider() and assumes BC semantics (e.g., passing it as a named Provider for BC-specific algorithms) silently gets the Sun provider instead and fails at runtime with NoSuchAlgorithmException rather than a clear error; users of authz-client embedded in apps that also pull keycloak-common utilities are bitten.

[ADVISORY] The authz-client jar now ships a CryptoProvider service registration with order 100, and the accompanying CryptoIntegration change makes lower-order providers silently ignorable, so an application that embeds authz-client alongside keycloak server artifacts in one classpath silently changes which crypto provider server code uses. If the authz-client jar leaks into a Keycloak-server-adjacent classpath (fat WARs, shared lib dirs), the order-based selection makes the conflict invisible: previously the duplicate-registration would have thrown and forced the operator to clean the classpath; now server crypto operations (FIPS mode included) can silently resolve to a different provider depending on jar presence, with no log at default level.

[ADVISORY] Adding a required order() method to the public CryptoProvider interface is a silent breaking change to all third-party/out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementations, which fail to compile or fail ServiceLoader loading once this lands. Any custom crypto provider written against the previous interface now throws ServiceConfigurationError ('Provider ... not a subtype') or a compile error, breaking custom-FIPS/custom-HSM integrations at upgrade time with no migration note in the diff; the interface change is incidental to the stated PR intent (add an authz-client provider) and was never the announced objective.

[ADVISORY] Replacing the hard failure on multiple discovered CryptoProviders with silent highest-order selection turns a fail-closed classpath integrity check into fail-open. Any dependency jar that transitively ships a META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider entry with a high order() silently replaces the FIPS-validated or BouncyCastle provider at runtime; a FIPS deployment operator gets no error and unknowingly runs on a non-validated crypto stack (e.g., AuthzClientCryptoProvider, whose getSignature/getAesGcmCipher simply throw, or a weaker third-party provider), whereas the old code aborted startup with IllegalStateException.

[ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create() calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), which initializes a shared (static/cached) crypto provider selection for the whole JVM/classloader from a client library entry point. In a servlet container where multiple webapps share a parent classloader containing keycloak-common, one application calling AuthzClient.create() pins the JVM-wide CryptoIntegration to whatever the authz-client classloader resolves (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, order 100), breaking other applications that rely on the full provider (FIPS mode, BouncyCastle-backed signature/PBKDF2 paths throw UnsupportedOperationException) — a cross-app crypto-configuration hijack that also silently downgrades a FIPS deployment.

[ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS performs no canonical-DER validation: it accepts non-minimal integer encodings, negative INTEGERs (high bit set), trailing garbage after the sequence, and does not range-check r/s against the curve order. JWT/applications accepting ECDSA signatures via this converter treat multiple distinct DER encodings as the same concatenated r||s value (signature malleability), which breaks any single-use or audit logic keyed on signature bytes and lets a captured signature be re-encoded to bypass naive replay/dedup checks; it also never rejects out-of-range values that the JOSE/JWS ECDSA spec forbids.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK's default KeyStore provider rather than any BouncyCastle provider, misrepresenting the JVM's crypto stack to callers that branch on this value. Code paths in keycloak-common that call getProvider().getName() to decide whether BouncyCastle-backed algorithms are available (e.g., for PBKDF2, PKCS keystore handling, or FIPS detection) will take the BC-available branch on a plain JDK and then fail or fall back to weaker defaults, since the returned provider is not BC at all.

[BUG] The test never asserts that concatenatedRSToASN1DER's output matches the original Java-generated ASN.1 DER signature `sign`; it only asserts a round-trip of the concatenated form. concatenatedRSToASN1DER could emit malformed or semantically wrong DER (wrong tags, wrong lengths, mangled r/s values) and the test still passes, because asn1derToConcatenatedRS is then applied to that same wrong output and the two conversions cancel each other out — a classic mirror-test where both functions are only checked against each other, not against the spec/real Signature output. A regression in the encoder ships to every authz-client user using ES256/384/512 signatures while the suite stays green; the fix is to assert ArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des) or verify the converted signature with Signature.verify.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and the s one) whose output is discarded; only the third encoder inside writeDerSeq is used. Any future reader debugging signature conversion traces dead encoder calls that produce no output; the two discarded calls imply side effects that do not exist and obscure that only the writeDerSeq result matters — deleting both lines changes nothing behaviorally, which is the deletion test passing.

[ADVISORY] The single generated EC keypair is shared across all three algorithm tests and the test data path exercises only whatever r/s values the JVM's random keygen happens to produce, so edge cases like r or s smaller than len/2 (leading zero truncation in integerToBytes) are exercised only by chance. The integerToBytes length-adjustment branches (both the qLength < bytes.length and qLength > bytes.length arms) have no deterministic test trigger — a run can pass or fail depending on random BigIntegers drawn, so a regression in padding logic produces a flaky test rather than a reliable failure, and CI greens can mask an intermittent signature-corruption bug.

[BUG] order() is added to the public CryptoProvider SPI interface with no default method, so every existing third-party CryptoProvider implementation fails when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls CryptoProvider::order to sort the ServiceLoader results. Any deployment with a custom (out-of-tree) crypto provider that compiled against the old interface throws AbstractMethodError inside detectProvider at first CryptoIntegration.getProvider() call — previously-working deployments now fail at startup/request time with an obscure AbstractMethodError instead of a migration message.

[BUG] Provider selection by order() has no deterministic tie-breaker, and DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all declare order()==200, so when two providers coexist on one classloader the winner is decided by ServiceLoader iteration (classpath) order, not by configuration. A FIPS deployment where the default provider leaks onto the classpath alongside fips1402 (previously caught by the explicit 'Multiple crypto providers' IllegalStateException) now silently picks one of the two arbitrarily — possibly the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider — and only logs the ignored provider at debug level, so a FIPS compliance requirement is silently violated with no error surfaced.

[ADVISORY] The old hard failure on multiple providers is replaced by silently returning the highest-order provider with only a debug-level log listing the ignored ones. Operators who previously got a loud IllegalStateException on a polluted classpath (e.g., a duplicated provider across a fat-jar) now get non-FIPS or unintended crypto behavior with no warning at any production log level; the misconfiguration is invisible unless debug logging is enabled.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of KeyStore.getDefaultType() (typically the JDK 'sun' provider), not a BouncyCastle provider, despite the method contract and name. Any caller in the authz-client path that uses CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC (e.g., for PEM parsing or provider-specific algorithm instantiation) silently gets the JDK default provider and either works by accident or fails with a NoSuchAlgorithmException that misdirects debugging toward a missing BouncyCastle dependency.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs and discards two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) and .write(sBigInteger)) whose outputs are never used before the real encoder below. Pure dead work per signature conversion; the next maintainer reading the method must determine whether those lines are load-bearing before changing the encoding logic, adding comprehension risk for zero benefit — both lines can be deleted outright.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add a ServiceLoader registration in authz-client (META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider) for AuthzClientCryptoProvider, and CryptoIntegration.detectProvider is changed to no longer fail on multiple providers but instead sort by CryptoProvider::order and pick the first. AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements CryptoProvider but throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods, so making it globally discoverable can be risky if it is ever selected. However, in this diff it is explicitly given a lower order (100) than the main providers updated here (DefaultCryptoProvider/WildFlyElytronProvider/FIPS1402Provider all 200), so when those are present it should not be selected, weakening the finding’s claim that it will commonly be picked “alongside or instead of” the intended provider. The concern is still real and grounded (global service exposure + partial implementation + removal of the multiple-provider hard guard), but it’s not a directly verifiable functional break from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Ties in provider order() are resolved by ServiceLoader iteration order, making provider selection classpath-order dependent. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so any classpath carrying two of them (e.g. default + fips1402) previously failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' and now silently picks whichever the ServiceLoader enumerates first — a FIPS deployment can silently boot on the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider with no error or warning above debug level.

adjudication.rationale: In CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(), providers are now sorted by order() desc and the first is selected even when multiple exist; the previous hard-fail on multiple providers was removed. Since DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200 in this diff, ties will be resolved by the (stable) sort’s encounter order, which comes from ServiceLoader iteration/classpath order. The only notice about ignored providers is logger.debugf, so a deployment with multiple providers can silently pick an unintended one (e.g., non-FIPS) with no warning/error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new provider-sorting/selection behavior has no test anywhere in the diff. The diff changes a hard failure (multiple providers = IllegalStateException) into ordered selection and adds the order() contract to a public interface, but no test covers sorting, tie behavior, or the 'Ignored crypto providers' path; a regression in the comparator or the ServiceLoader enumeration breaks provider selection for every embedding (server and authz-client) with nothing to catch it. The only new test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) exercises ECDSA byte conversion, not provider detection.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes provider detection semantics in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` from throwing on multiple `CryptoProvider`s to sorting by the new `CryptoProvider.order()` (descending) and selecting the first, with an added “Ignored crypto providers” debug path. It also adds `order()` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface and implements it across providers (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, and new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`). The only added test (`ECDSAAlgorithmTest`) exercises ECDSA signature conversion logic in `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider()`, not ServiceLoader sorting/selection, tie/ordering behavior, or the ignored-providers logging branch. That’s a concrete, diff-grounded missing test for newly introduced nontrivial selection logic, not a direct functional defect shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The only test of concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a round-trip through the same provider's own decoder, so it cannot detect a DER encoding both methods get wrong in the same way. The test converts DER→concat→DER→concat and asserts the two concat forms match; if concatenatedRSToASN1DER emitted non-interoperable DER (wrong tag/length) while asn1derToConcatenatedRS parsed it back symmetrically, the test passes but a Keycloak server or any BC-based verifier rejects the produced JOSE signature. A test asserting the re-encoded DER verifies against the keyPair public key (or equals the original raw DER signature bytes) is the missing acceptance criterion.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` only asserts a symmetric round-trip using the same new implementation: it takes the JVM/JCA-produced DER signature (`signature.sign()`), converts it via `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`, re-encodes via `concatenatedRSToASN1DER`, then decodes again and compares only the concatenated forms (`Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)`). This can pass even if `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` produces DER that is not interoperable, as long as the paired `ASN1Decoder`/`asn1derToConcatenatedRS` accepts it. The diff does not include an acceptance check like verifying the re-encoded DER with `Signature#verify` using `keyPair.getPublic()` or comparing the re-encoded DER bytes to the original `sign` output.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM's default KeyStore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider, so the method's contract is silently violated. Any caller that uses CryptoIntegration in a process where the authz-client provider wins (standalone client, order 100 < 200 so only when no other provider exists) and requests the BouncyCastle provider gets e.g. SUN with no BC algorithms; code doing provider-lookup by BC OID or name fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException at runtime instead of at selection time.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns the JVM’s default KeyStore provider (typically `SUN`/`SunJSSE`), not a BouncyCastle `Provider`. This contradicts the `CryptoProvider` method contract/name (`getBouncyCastleProvider`) and would cause runtime failures for code paths that expect BC-specific algorithms when the authz-client provider is selected (it can be selected when no higher-order providers are present, per the new `order()` selection logic in `CryptoIntegration`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] readLength's bounds check compares the declared length against the total input size (limit), not the remaining bytes (limit - count), so it only rejects lengths that overshoot the entire buffer. For a nested element near the end of a corrupted signature, a length that overruns the current element but stays under the total buffer passes readLength and fails later in read() with a generic EOF IOException (or reads sibling bytes as content), losing the 'corrupted stream - out of bounds length' diagnostic and making malformed-signature errors harder to attribute; no test covers the overlong-length path.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ASN1Decoder.readLength()`, the bounds check is `if (length >= limit)` where `limit` is the total input size (`bytes.length`), not the remaining bytes in the stream (or remaining bytes within the current container). This means a declared length that exceeds what’s left to read but is still < total buffer size won’t be rejected as “out of bounds” at length-parse time and will instead fail later in `read(int)` with a generic EOF/other misparse behavior. The diff also only adds a happy-path ECDSA round-trip test (`ECDSAAlgorithmTest`) and no malformed/overlong-length tests, matching the finding’s test-coverage note.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The diff silently deletes the hard failure on multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath, converting a startup misconfiguration error into a debug-level log line, changing server-wide behavior far beyond the stated authz-client intent. A Keycloak server deployment that previously refused to boot with two crypto providers on the classpath (an explicit safety check against ambiguous FIPS/non-FIPS crypto) now boots silently using whichever provider has the highest order(); operators running an unintended FIPS-ineligible provider get non-compliant crypto with no error, only a debug log they will never see at default log levels.

adjudication.rationale: The diff verifiably changes behavior in CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(): it no longer throws when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are present, instead it sorts by CryptoProvider::order (new API) and returns the highest, logging the rest at debug (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). This is a significant behavior/policy change (misconfiguration no longer hard-fails), but the introduction of CryptoProvider.order() and its implementation in the built-in providers (default/elytron/fips all return 200; authz-client provider returns 100) indicates this selection behavior is intentional rather than an accidental defect. The concern about silent selection/log level is valid as a review issue, but it’s not clearly a “bug” given the explicit new ordering mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Adding the abstract method order() to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation breaks every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation at runtime with AbstractMethodError. Third-party or customer custom crypto providers compiled against the old interface load fine but throw AbstractMethodError when detectProvider's sorted() comparator invokes order(), turning a previously-working deployment into a runtime failure after upgrade; the diff shows no default method or migration note for external implementers.
matched_golden_ids: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly flags that adding an abstract order() method to the public CryptoProvider interface (without a default implementation) will break existing third-party implementations at runtime (AbstractMethodError), which is the same backward-compatibility concern described in the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs and discards two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances with their BigInteger writes before building the real sequence, dead code with no traceable requirement. The next maintainer reading the method assumes the two orphaned encoders (ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) lines) have an effect and preserves or 'fixes' them; deleting both lines changes nothing, failing the deletion test's bar for dead weight.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK default KeyStore provider rather than a BouncyCastle provider, a misleading near-no-op that will surprise any caller that trusts the method contract. Any code path in authz-client (or shared common code) that calls getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC-specific behavior (e.g., BC-only PKCS12 handling or EC curve support) silently gets the Sun provider instead; the method name promises something the implementation does not deliver and no caller in the diff exercises it.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e., whatever provider backs the JDK default keystore type, not an explicit BouncyCastle provider. Given the `CryptoProvider` API method name/contract (`getBouncyCastleProvider`) and the fact other implementations return an actual BC/BCFIPS provider (or `null`), this is a concrete contract mismatch introduced by the diff and can lead to incorrect behavior if callers rely on BC-specific capabilities.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS accepts indefinite-length DER sequences because readSequence's `while (length > 0)` loop is skipped when readLength() returns -1, silently returning an empty list that then fails the size!=2 check instead of rejecting indefinite encoding explicitly. A caller passing a BER indefinite-length signature gets a generic 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' IOException instead of a precise indefinite-length rejection, complicating diagnosis; the bound also means a truncated first element that overruns the declared length reads past the sequence into following bytes rather than failing, but the final arraycopy bounds are the safety net.

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readSequence(), readLength() can return -1 for indefinite-length (0x80). The current loop `while (length > 0)` will be skipped and returns an empty `List<byte[]>` without explicitly rejecting indefinite-length encoding. In the shown usage (AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS), this still results in a failure via `seq.size() != 2`, but with a generic message rather than a precise “indefinite length not allowed” error. Also, readSequence does not enforce that each element fits within the remaining declared sequence length (it relies only on the overall `limit`), which can cause parsing to read past the sequence boundary into trailing bytes if present, though it will typically still fail later for ECDSA (size!=2 / EOF). This is a real, diff-grounded robustness/diagnostics issue, but not a demonstrated functional acceptance/bypass in the code path shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The tests only verify the round-trip concatenatedRS -> ASN1DER -> concatenatedRS, never validating the ASN.1 DER output against a known-good encoding, so an encoder bug that round-trips consistently (e.g., non-minimal DER integer encoding) passes the suite. If ASN1Encoder emits non-canonical DER (e.g., negative or non-minimal INTEGER encodings), a real Keycloak server verifying the JWS will reject the signature while the diff's own tests stay green; the happy-path round trip cannot represent cross-implementation compatibility, which is the whole point of the ECDSA signature conversion.

adjudication.rationale: The added test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` only checks a self-consistency round-trip using the same implementation (`asn1derToConcatenatedRS` -> `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` -> `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`) and never compares the produced DER against any known-good/canonical encoding or an independent verifier. This is grounded in the diff: the test asserts only `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2);` and does not validate DER conformance/cross-implementation compatibility. While the diff does not prove `ASN1Encoder` is non-canonical, the finding correctly identifies a specific test gap for newly added ASN.1 DER logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Adding a non-default abstract method `order()` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface breaks every existing third-party implementer at runtime with AbstractMethodError. Any out-of-tree CryptoProvider compiled against the old interface (SPI is a documented extension point — custom/alternative crypto deployments register via META-INF/services) now fails when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` invokes `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` on it during `CryptoIntegration.init`, which the diff makes AuthzClient.create call unconditionally — the previously-working authz client and the whole Keycloak startup path crash with AbstractMethodError instead of a versioned contract change. The method should have been a Java default method returning a sentinel.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new non-default abstract method `int order()` to the public SPI interface `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` and immediately uses it in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` via `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)`. Any third-party `CryptoProvider` implementation compiled against the previous version of the interface will not have this method, and when loaded by `ServiceLoader` and sorted, calling `order()` will trigger `AbstractMethodError` at runtime. This is a binary compatibility break introduced by the diff; making `order()` a `default` method would avoid it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff replaces the fail-fast 'multiple crypto providers on classpath' error with silent preference by order(), turning a previously-loud misconfiguration into a silent one, and ties are resolved nondeterministically. Operators who accidentally end up with two providers on the classpath (e.g. authz-client fat-jar plus the server's DefaultCryptoProvider) previously got an explicit IllegalStateException naming the conflict; now the loser is only a debug-level log line, so a deployment that silently routes crypto through the wrong provider ships to production. Additionally, three in-tree providers all return order()==200 (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider), so if two of them coexist the ServiceLoader iteration order — which is classpath-order dependent and unstable — decides which crypto stack (FIPS vs non-FIPS) is used, a selection no configuration controls.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() removes the previous fail-fast IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found, and instead sorts providers by order() (descending) and returns the first while only logging ignored providers at debug level. This is a real operability/architecture concern: an accidental extra provider on the classpath would no longer surface loudly. Also, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order()==200 in this diff, so when more than one of them is present, the comparator treats them as equal and the chosen provider depends on ServiceLoader encounter order (classpath/service file order), which is not explicitly controlled here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClientCryptoProvider registers itself as a classpath-wide CryptoProvider service while 14 of its 19 methods throw UnsupportedOperationException, and getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default KeyStore provider rather than BouncyCastle. Any application that has authz-client on its classpath alongside another CryptoProvider of lower order (any third-party provider with order < 100, which is all pre-existing ones given they lack order() — though those already fail per the interface break; or a future low-order one) silently routes all crypto through a provider whose getPemUtils/getSignature/getCertificateUtils throw. Within authz-client itself, any code path beyond ECDSA signature conversion — e.g. PEM parsing of a client's signing key or the JWT client-credential flow — now calls into these stubs and crashes at runtime. The getBouncyCastleProvider() lie is worse than an exception: callers (including BouncyIntegration-dependent code in common) get a plain SunJCE/SunRsaSign provider where BouncyCastle-specific algorithm OIDs or the BC keystore format is required, producing NoSuchAlgorithmException far from the cause.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (registered via `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`) and changes `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` to call `CryptoIntegration.init(...)`, which will auto-detect a `CryptoProvider` via `ServiceLoader`. The new provider implements `order()` as 100, but most required `CryptoProvider` methods throw `UnsupportedOperationException` (e.g., `getPemUtils`, `getSignature`, `getCertificateUtils`, etc.), meaning that if this provider is selected (e.g., when it’s the only provider on the classpath or it outranks another provider), crypto functionality beyond the ECDSA conversion helper will fail at runtime. Additionally, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` clearly does not return BouncyCastle; it returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is typically a default JDK provider, violating the method’s intent/contract and risking downstream failures that assume a BC provider.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The only test for the new ASN.1 DER codec is a self-referential round-trip through the same encoder/decoder under test, never verifying the produced DER against an independent parser or a real signature. A symmetric encoding bug — e.g. the encoder emitting a non-minimal INTEGER or the decoder's indefinite-length path (`readLength` returning -1 makes `readSequence`'s `while (length > 0)` loop return an empty list) being mirrored on both sides — keeps the test green while real-world signature verification against a spec-conformant verifier fails; the guard can be green while interop is broken. A cross-check against BouncyCastle's ASN1Primitive or an actual JWKS verification would close it.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` validates `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` against a real DER signature produced by `Signature.sign()`, but `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` is only validated by decoding its output with the same `ASN1Decoder` and comparing the concatenated RS (`rsConcat` vs `rsConcat2`). There is no independent verification that the produced DER is spec/interop-correct (e.g., verifying it with `Signature.verify()` or parsing with an independent ASN.1 library). Also, the decoder has an indefinite-length branch (`readLength()` returns `-1`) that `readSequence()` doesn’t handle (loop `while (length > 0)` would skip and return empty), which wouldn’t be caught by the current tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] readSequence treats an indefinite-length BER encoding (readLength returns -1) as an empty sequence and returns successfully instead of rejecting it. asn1derToConcatenatedRS fed an indefinite-length signature (BER, which some signers emit) returns no parse error of 'indefinite length' but instead proceeds to the size!=2 check, and more importantly the `while (length > 0)` loop exits immediately producing a misleading error message — or, if the length check were absent, silently empty output. A caller debugging gets 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' instead of the actual BER/DER mismatch, and any future reader of this method can be led to believe indefinite length is handled.
matched_golden_ids: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both comments flag the same root problem: `readLength` can return `-1` for indefinite-length BER, and the code does not properly handle that sentinel value, causing control-flow/arithmetic based on `length` to behave incorrectly (e.g., loop exits immediately / sequence treated as empty), leading to misleading or incorrect processing instead of rejecting indefinite length.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] This diff silently deletes the fail-fast 'multiple crypto providers on the classpath' IllegalStateException contract from CryptoIntegration.detectProvider, replacing it with order()-based silent selection, without any explicit acceptance of that behavioral change to server-side code. Previously, a misconfigured server classpath containing both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider (or elytron) threw an IllegalStateException at startup, telling the operator exactly which providers conflicted; now it silently picks the highest-order provider and only logs 'Ignored crypto providers' at DEBUG level. A FIPS-required deployment that accidentally also carries the non-FIPS jar now silently runs the non-FIPS provider (both have order 200, selection among ties is ServiceLoader order, i.e. non-deterministic across environments) — a compliance/security posture change invisible to the operator, and a contradiction of the method's documented purpose of detecting provider conflicts.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` to no longer throw when multiple `CryptoProvider`s are found (the previous `else if (foundProviders.size() > 1) { throw ... }` is removed). It now sorts by `CryptoProvider::order` descending and returns the first provider, only logging ignored providers at DEBUG. Since `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all implement `order()` as `200` in this diff, ties are not broken deterministically by the comparator, so provider selection with multiple jars present can be effectively dependent on `ServiceLoader` iteration order. This is a concrete behavioral change that can mask misconfiguration and lead to unpredictable provider choice.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK's default KeyStore provider, silently violating the CryptoProvider interface contract that this method returns the Bouncy Castle provider. Any common-code path that calls getBouncyCastleProvider() and assumes BC semantics (e.g., passing it as a named Provider for BC-specific algorithms) silently gets the Sun provider instead and fails at runtime with NoSuchAlgorithmException rather than a clear error; users of authz-client embedded in apps that also pull keycloak-common utilities are bitten.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the new AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements CryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider() as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which will typically return the JDK default keystore provider (e.g., SUN), not Bouncy Castle. Other CryptoProvider implementations in the diff (DefaultCryptoProvider/FIPS1402Provider) return an actual BC/BCFIPS provider, so this implementation is inconsistent with the method’s intended semantics and can cause runtime failures if callers use the returned Provider expecting BC capabilities.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The authz-client jar now ships a CryptoProvider service registration with order 100, and the accompanying CryptoIntegration change makes lower-order providers silently ignorable, so an application that embeds authz-client alongside keycloak server artifacts in one classpath silently changes which crypto provider server code uses. If the authz-client jar leaks into a Keycloak-server-adjacent classpath (fat WARs, shared lib dirs), the order-based selection makes the conflict invisible: previously the duplicate-registration would have thrown and forced the operator to clean the classpath; now server crypto operations (FIPS mode included) can silently resolve to a different provider depending on jar presence, with no log at default level.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add a CryptoProvider service entry in authz-client (META-INF/services/... -> AuthzClientCryptoProvider) with order()=100, and it changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to no longer throw when multiple providers are present; instead it sorts by CryptoProvider::order descending and silently picks the first, only logging ignored providers at DEBUG. That is a real behavioral/operational concern because classpath conflicts that previously failed fast are now hidden by default logging. However, the specific claim that authz-client would silently take over Keycloak server crypto provider is not supported by the diff as written: the server-side providers in this diff (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) all return order()=200, so they would outrank the authz-client provider (100) if co-present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Adding a required order() method to the public CryptoProvider interface is a silent breaking change to all third-party/out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementations, which fail to compile or fail ServiceLoader loading once this lands. Any custom crypto provider written against the previous interface now throws ServiceConfigurationError ('Provider ... not a subtype') or a compile error, breaking custom-FIPS/custom-HSM integrations at upgrade time with no migration note in the diff; the interface change is incidental to the stated PR intent (add an authz-client provider) and was never the announced objective.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new abstract method `int order();` to the public `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` interface (common/src/main/java/.../CryptoProvider.java) without providing a default implementation. This is a source/binary incompatible change for any third-party/out-of-tree `CryptoProvider` implementations compiled against the previous interface: they will fail to compile until they implement `order()`, and previously-built providers can fail at runtime when loaded via `ServiceLoader` because they no longer implement the updated interface. While in-repo providers were updated to implement `order()` (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and new AuthzClientCryptoProvider), external implementations are not, making the finding’s compatibility concern directly grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Replacing the hard failure on multiple discovered CryptoProviders with silent highest-order selection turns a fail-closed classpath integrity check into fail-open. Any dependency jar that transitively ships a META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider entry with a high order() silently replaces the FIPS-validated or BouncyCastle provider at runtime; a FIPS deployment operator gets no error and unknowingly runs on a non-validated crypto stack (e.g., AuthzClientCryptoProvider, whose getSignature/getAesGcmCipher simply throw, or a weaker third-party provider), whereas the old code aborted startup with IllegalStateException.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider from throwing IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProviders are discovered to instead sorting by the new CryptoProvider.order() (descending) and silently selecting the first (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). This removes a fail-closed integrity check and allows any additional jar on the classpath that provides META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider with a higher order() to override the intended provider without an error (only a debug log of “Ignored crypto providers”). That is a security-relevant behavioral regression directly introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create() calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), which initializes a shared (static/cached) crypto provider selection for the whole JVM/classloader from a client library entry point. In a servlet container where multiple webapps share a parent classloader containing keycloak-common, one application calling AuthzClient.create() pins the JVM-wide CryptoIntegration to whatever the authz-client classloader resolves (AuthzClientCryptoProvider, order 100), breaking other applications that rely on the full provider (FIPS mode, BouncyCastle-backed signature/PBKDF2 paths throw UnsupportedOperationException) — a cross-app crypto-configuration hijack that also silently downgrades a FIPS deployment.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show a new side effect: `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, which triggers global crypto-provider autodetection via `ServiceLoader` (`CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(classLoader)`). Because `CryptoIntegration` is a common module with (likely) shared static state (implied by `getProvider()` and `init(...)` API), initializing it from a client-library entry point can create classloader/initialization-order coupling in multi-app containers. However, the finding’s claim that this will necessarily pin to `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (order 100) and downgrade FIPS is not guaranteed by the diff: `detectProvider` now sorts by `CryptoProvider::order` descending, and the built-in providers in this diff (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`) all return `order() == 200`, so they would win over `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` if visible to that classloader. The cross-app “hijack” scenario depends on classloader visibility and static caching behavior not shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] asn1derToConcatenatedRS performs no canonical-DER validation: it accepts non-minimal integer encodings, negative INTEGERs (high bit set), trailing garbage after the sequence, and does not range-check r/s against the curve order. JWT/applications accepting ECDSA signatures via this converter treat multiple distinct DER encodings as the same concatenated r||s value (signature malleability), which breaks any single-use or audit logic keyed on signature bytes and lets a captured signature be re-encoded to bypass naive replay/dedup checks; it also never rejects out-of-range values that the JOSE/JWS ECDSA spec forbids.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` implementation, `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` uses the custom `ASN1Decoder` (`readSequence()` + `readInteger()`) which does not enforce canonical DER constraints: `readInteger()` accepts any INTEGER encoding (including leading 0x00 padding) and can produce negative `BigInteger` values; `readSequence()` does not verify the input is fully consumed so trailing bytes after the SEQUENCE would be ignored. There is also no explicit range check for r/s. However, from the diff alone it’s not verifiable that this method is ever fed attacker-controlled DER (it may only decode DER produced by `Signature.sign()`), so the claimed security impact in JWT usage can’t be confirmed just from this PR.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK's default KeyStore provider rather than any BouncyCastle provider, misrepresenting the JVM's crypto stack to callers that branch on this value. Code paths in keycloak-common that call getProvider().getName() to decide whether BouncyCastle-backed algorithms are available (e.g., for PBKDF2, PKCS keystore handling, or FIPS detection) will take the BC-available branch on a plain JDK and then fail or fall back to weaker defaults, since the returned provider is not BC at all.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (added in `authz/client/src/main/java/.../AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java`), `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e., the JDK KeyStore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider. Given the interface contract/name (`CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()`), this misrepresents the available crypto provider to any caller that relies on it for BC-specific behavior. This behavior is directly verifiable from the diff and constitutes incorrect implementation (and can lead to wrong branching/feature detection).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The test never asserts that concatenatedRSToASN1DER's output matches the original Java-generated ASN.1 DER signature `sign`; it only asserts a round-trip of the concatenated form. concatenatedRSToASN1DER could emit malformed or semantically wrong DER (wrong tags, wrong lengths, mangled r/s values) and the test still passes, because asn1derToConcatenatedRS is then applied to that same wrong output and the two conversions cancel each other out — a classic mirror-test where both functions are only checked against each other, not against the spec/real Signature output. A regression in the encoder ships to every authz-client user using ES256/384/512 signatures while the suite stays green; the fix is to assert ArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des) or verify the converted signature with Signature.verify.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ECDSAAlgorithmTest`, the assertion only checks a round-trip on the concatenated R||S form: `sign` (DER) -> `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` -> `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` -> `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`, and then `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)`. It never asserts that `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` reproduces the original Java-generated DER signature (`sign`) or that the re-encoded DER verifies via `Signature.verify`, so an encoder/decoder pair that are mutually consistent but spec-incompatible could still pass.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and the s one) whose output is discarded; only the third encoder inside writeDerSeq is used. Any future reader debugging signature conversion traces dead encoder calls that produce no output; the two discarded calls imply side effects that do not exist and obscure that only the writeDerSeq result matters — deleting both lines changes nothing behaviorally, which is the deletion test passing.
matched_golden_ids: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes the same dead-code problem: two ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to but their outputs are discarded, while the actual encoding result comes only from a separate encoder used in the return/writeDerSeq call. This matches the golden comment’s concern about useless earlier operations being rendered irrelevant by the subsequent encoding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The single generated EC keypair is shared across all three algorithm tests and the test data path exercises only whatever r/s values the JVM's random keygen happens to produce, so edge cases like r or s smaller than len/2 (leading zero truncation in integerToBytes) are exercised only by chance. The integerToBytes length-adjustment branches (both the qLength < bytes.length and qLength > bytes.length arms) have no deterministic test trigger — a run can pass or fail depending on random BigIntegers drawn, so a regression in padding logic produces a flaky test rather than a reliable failure, and CI greens can mask an intermittent signature-corruption bug.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added ECDSAAlgorithmTest, the signature values (and thus r/s BigIntegers) come from real ECDSA signing (Signature.sign()) and a freshly generated EC keypair, so the test does not deterministically exercise edge cases in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider#integerToBytes (the qLength < bytes.length truncation and qLength > bytes.length left-padding branches). That means regressions affecting only leading-zero/padding/truncation scenarios could slip through CI because the test’s coverage depends on whatever r/s values happen to be produced. However, the finding’s claim that a “single generated EC keypair is shared across all three algorithm tests” is not supported: with JUnit4 each @Test method runs on a new test instance, so the constructor generates a new keypair per test method, not one shared across all three.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] order() is added to the public CryptoProvider SPI interface with no default method, so every existing third-party CryptoProvider implementation fails when CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls CryptoProvider::order to sort the ServiceLoader results. Any deployment with a custom (out-of-tree) crypto provider that compiled against the old interface throws AbstractMethodError inside detectProvider at first CryptoIntegration.getProvider() call — previously-working deployments now fail at startup/request time with an obscure AbstractMethodError instead of a migration message.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new abstract method `int order();` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface (no `default` implementation). `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` now sorts `ServiceLoader` results via `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)`, which will invoke `order()` on every loaded provider. Any out-of-tree `CryptoProvider` implementation compiled against the previous interface will not have this method and will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `detectProvider` runs, breaking previously working deployments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Provider selection by order() has no deterministic tie-breaker, and DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all declare order()==200, so when two providers coexist on one classloader the winner is decided by ServiceLoader iteration (classpath) order, not by configuration. A FIPS deployment where the default provider leaks onto the classpath alongside fips1402 (previously caught by the explicit 'Multiple crypto providers' IllegalStateException) now silently picks one of the two arbitrarily — possibly the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider — and only logs the ignored provider at debug level, so a FIPS compliance requirement is silently violated with no error surfaced.

adjudication.rationale: In CryptoIntegration.detectProvider, the previous behavior throwing IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProvider implementations were found was removed. The new logic sorts providers by CryptoProvider::order descending and returns the first, only logging “Ignored crypto providers” at debug level when more than one exists. In the diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order()==200, so when multiple of these are present, the sort provides no tie-breaker and the chosen provider depends on ServiceLoader iteration/classpath order rather than an explicit configuration. This can silently select a non-FIPS provider even when a FIPS provider is present, which is a real behavior/safety regression introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The old hard failure on multiple providers is replaced by silently returning the highest-order provider with only a debug-level log listing the ignored ones. Operators who previously got a loud IllegalStateException on a polluted classpath (e.g., a duplicated provider across a fat-jar) now get non-FIPS or unintended crypto behavior with no warning at any production log level; the misconfiguration is invisible unless debug logging is enabled.

adjudication.rationale: In common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java, the previous hard failure on multiple CryptoProvider instances (`throw new IllegalStateException(...)`) was removed. The new logic sorts by `CryptoProvider::order` and returns the first provider, while only emitting `logger.debugf(...)` messages about the selected provider and any ignored ones. This means a polluted/duplicated classpath (multiple providers present) no longer fails fast and can silently pick an unintended provider with no warning at non-debug log levels, which can lead to incorrect or non-compliant crypto behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of KeyStore.getDefaultType() (typically the JDK 'sun' provider), not a BouncyCastle provider, despite the method contract and name. Any caller in the authz-client path that uses CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC (e.g., for PEM parsing or provider-specific algorithm instantiation) silently gets the JDK default provider and either works by accident or fails with a NoSuchAlgorithmException that misdirects debugging toward a missing BouncyCastle dependency.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` as a `CryptoProvider` (registered via `META-INF/services/...CryptoProvider`). Its `getBouncyCastleProvider()` implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the provider for the default JDK keystore type (typically a JDK/Sun provider), not a BouncyCastle provider, contradicting the interface contract/method name (`CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()`). With `AuthzClient.create()` now calling `CryptoIntegration.init(...)`, this provider can be selected on the authz-client classpath, so any code using `CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider()` would receive the wrong provider and could fail/misbehave.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER constructs and discards two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) and .write(sBigInteger)) whose outputs are never used before the real encoder below. Pure dead work per signature conversion; the next maintainer reading the method must determine whether those lines are load-bearing before changing the encoding logic, adding comprehension risk for zero benefit — both lines can be deleted outright.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` each create a new ASN1Encoder, write into its internal buffer, and then discard the instance without using `toByteArray()` or passing it onward. The actual returned encoding is built by a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(...)` call below, so these two earlier encoder instances are pure dead work and can be removed for clarity and minor performance.
